name: Buff
lede: Buff is a light, warm yellow-tan named for buffalo leather, the soldier's coat color that George Washington carried into the American Revolution as half of buff and blue.

sections.title: A leather before a color
sections.body:
*Buff* is slang, clipped from *buffalo*. Through the sixteenth century and into the early seventeenth, it meant a buttery tanned ox leather, a thicker and tougher cousin of what we now call chamois [2]. Paterson's dictionary defines the color as a pale yellowish brown or a light yellow, the shade of buff leather, and adds that the leather's likeness to bare skin gave English the phrase "in the buff", meaning naked [1].

Buff is a color name from the animal world. In the count of English color names that Garfield reports from Deane Judd of the US National Bureau of Standards, 133 of roughly 7,500 names came from animals, and buff is the example given [3].

The swatch here, #FFC680, is a light orange-yellow [4]. Our library finds it in the ISCC-NBS name charts of 1955 and in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, and its nearest ISCC-NBS name, light orange yellow, lies 5.1 units away [4]. Another screen buff, from the xkcd survey of 2010, is #FEF69E, a much paler lemon [4]. The word has never pointed at one paint chip, and Paterson's own wording, anything from light yellow to yellowish brown, allows for that [1].

sections.title: The soldier's coat
sections.body:
Soldiers across Europe in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries were issued heavy buff-leather coats, which often stood in for metal armor and were sometimes worn beneath chain mail for padding [2]. The leather also made fashionable jerkins and doublets, yet it was fighting that people mostly linked with it [2]. Cavalry wore buff coats in that period [2].

When armor stopped mattering, the color stayed. Around the middle of the 1700s, buff breeches had become a must for any well-dressed European gentleman, while light tans lingered in military uniform through the nineteenth century, chiefly as facings on bolder coats [2]. In the years of the guillotine, scarlet gowns and crimson velvet coats turned distasteful, even dangerous in France, and plain clothes such as buff breeches took their place [5]. Buff was the safe color of a nervous age. For the red it was avoiding, see [[flower:madder|madder]] and [[scarlet]].

sections.title: Buff and blue
sections.body:
The color's most famous turn came in the American Revolution [2]. George Washington had fought for Britain, in scarlet, in the Seven Years' War [2]. Delegates meeting at the Second Continental Congress in the summer of 1775 saw him in the buff and blue of the Fairfax Independent Company of Volunteers [2]. John Adams wrote to his wife Abigail that Colonel Washington's uniform and military experience were of great service to the delegates [2]. He was made commander in chief on the spot, and from then on he put his soldiers in buff and blue whenever cloth allowed [2].

A letter of 22 April 1777, about his personal guard, shows how personal the choice was [2]. He told Captain Caleb Gibbs that he preferred blue and buff because it was the uniform he wore himself, and that any other color would do, red excepted [2].

From there the pair became a badge of liberty. Across the Atlantic, Whigs led by Edmund Burke and Charles James Fox took up Washington's colors as a sign of sympathy with American independence [2]. Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire, canvassed for the Whigs in buff and blue and dressed her footmen at Chatsworth in the same pair [2]. In 1961, at a Bermuda summit, Prime Minister Harold Macmillan presented John F. Kennedy with silver buttons taken from that livery [2].

Cloth in the right colors was hard to find. When HMS *Symmetry* was captured on New Year's Day 1778 with scarlet, blue and buff cloth for the army's officers aboard, St Clair's notes record general rejoicing, followed by a squabble over where the cloth would end up [2].

sections.title: Buff Orange in the naturalists' chart
sections.body:
Before buff was a fashion it was a naturalist's tool. In Syme's 1821 edition of Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours*, *Buff Orange* is number 77 in the chart of yellows and oranges, and its recipe is sienna yellow with a little Dutch orange [6]. Syme's examples from nature are the streak beside a kingfisher's eye, the stamens of the large white cistus, and the mineral natrolite [6]. A buff hibiscus is cited under the next-but-two entry, Reddish Orange [6].

By that recipe Syme's buff was closer to an orange than to the pale tan the word names today [6]. The color library still holds both ends of the family, [[buff-orange]] and [[buff-yellow]], as close neighbors of this swatch [4]. If you want a buff to look at in the real world, the pale feathers around a kingfisher's eye are as good a place as the naturalists thought [6].

sections.title: Among its neighbors
sections.body:
Buff sits in a crowd of pale warm neutrals: [[tan]], [[camel]], [[apricot]], [[beige]] and [[khaki]]. Pastoureau notes one earlier crowd of the same kind. The yellow called Nankin, highly prized from the 1740s to the 1770s, covered a wide range from light yellow to nearly orange, passing through blond, straw, buff and beige, and its common trait was to be luminous without being saturated [7].

Painters use the word loosely too. Jarman, writing as an artist rather than a historian, notes that Geertgen tot Sint Jans painted flesh in a buff-pink in *The Nativity at Night* [9]. The same writer ties buff to buffalo hide and, more darkly, to death and slaughter, which is a poet's association and not a documented one [9].

sections.title: Words, appetite and a latte
sections.body:
Buff names the color in three unrelated words. One is the leather. Another is the enthusiast, as in the "film buffs" of Pastoureau's pages on black-and-white cinema, which has no color meaning at all [13]. A third is the verb to buff, to polish.

The mid-century color-psychology writer Birren listed buff among the true appetite colors, with peach, red, orange, brown, warm yellow and clear green [8]. He suggested buff highlights on gray machinery to mark working parts, and warned that a home or office surrounded by nothing but ivory or buff would wear on a person's disposition [8]. That is period opinion, not tested evidence.

The name turned up once more in cosmology. When two scientists surveyed over 200,000 galaxies and found that the universe as a whole is a shade of beige, they went looking for a livelier name; "big bang buff" was among the suggestions, and "cosmic latte" won [10].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Buff is not a common painted color. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 75 works, and the match is most often a light area, a highlight, in 95 per cent of them [11]. The earliest is Fra Angelico's *Tabernacle of the Linaioli* of 1432, where it covers 18 per cent [11]. The largest share belongs to Tamechika Reizei's *Twelve Poetic Immortals and Their Poems* of 1845, where it fills 82 per cent of the picture [11]. Sakai Hōitsu's [[painting:cma-140476|Paulownias and Chrysanthemums]] and other Japanese works are among the leaders, which suggests that the match is often the painted ground, though we did not measure that [11].

The surprises are in the rates. Only three of the 47 works by [[painter:albrecht-durer|Dürer]] in the archive carry a buff patch, but that is about twenty times the expected rate [11]. The twentieth century is also high, with 12 of 1,674 paintings, 2.3 times the baseline, and the 1910s peak with 6 of 523 [11]. Germany, with 7 of 692 paintings, and Japan, with 6 of 698, are the countries that stand out [11]. The colors that most often share a canvas with it are [[tan]] and [[camel]] [11]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen color, not a pigment test [11].

In Google Books the word *buff* peaks around 1929, but the curve mixes the color, the enthusiast and the polish, so it is not a history of the color alone [12].

origin.first_recorded: as a leather name in the 1500s and early 1600s; as a color name later (exact date undocumented here)
origin.source: St Clair, Secret Lives of Color, 'Buff'; Paterson, Dictionary of Colour

questions.q: Where does the color name buff come from?
choices: A town where the dye was made

questions.q: True or false: the phrase "in the buff" comes from Washington's uniform.
Which two colors made up the uniform Washington preferred?

openers: Buff began as a leather: soldiers wore buff coats where later armies wore armor or none.
Washington asked for blue and buff because it was the uniform he wore himself, and any color but red would do.
Look at the feathers around a kingfisher's eye: naturalists two centuries ago used them to define buff orange.
